kiddushin-8b-2-2.note: The sons of Rav Huna bar Avin agreed to buy a maidservant for copper coins. They had no money yet, so they handed over a piece of silver as a pledge. When her price went up, the sellers tried to cancel the sale, and Rabbi Ami ruled that there was no valid purchase at all, since the money was never actually paid and a pledge does not transfer ownership.

terms.meaning: Small copper coins, the smallest unit of money in the Talmud's law.
An item held as a pledge, which does not by itself make a sale final.

kiddushin-8b-2-2.why: Rav Naḥman has just ruled that a man who promises a hundred dinars for betrothal but hands over only collateral has given nothing; this purchase case shows the same principle, that collateral is not payment, applied to a sale.

kiddushin-8b-14-14.note: A man selling glass beads offered a woman a string of them on the condition that she become betrothed (engaged) to him by accepting it. She answered, 'Give, give.' Rav Hama ruled that this phrase means nothing: she was not agreeing to the condition, so no betrothal took place.

terms.meaning: Kiddushin, the formal act of engagement, which legally makes a woman a man's wife.

kiddushin-8b-14-14.why: The Gemara is listing replies a woman might make when a man offers her something as betrothal, such as 'Give it to a dog' or 'to a poor person'. This opens a run of three similar cases about doubled words.

kiddushin-9a-1-1.note: A man drinking wine in a shop was asked by a woman for a cup. He asked her whether, if he gave it to her, she would be betrothed to him with it. She replied, 'Give to drink, give it to me to drink.' Rav Hama ruled this reply means nothing, so she was not betrothed.

terms.meaning: Kiddushin, the formal act of engagement, which legally makes a woman a man's wife.

kiddushin-9a-1-1.why: It follows the glass-bead seller as a second case of a woman's doubled words; the Gemara then asks what happens if she says the word only once, and rules that she is still not betrothed.

kiddushin-9a-2-2.note: A man picking dates was asked by a woman to throw her two. He asked whether, if he threw them, she would be betrothed to him with them, and she answered, 'Throw, throw.' Rav Zevid ruled that this phrase means nothing and she was not betrothed.
kiddushin-9a-2-2.why: It is the third in a run of cases about a woman repeating a word when offered betrothal; right after it the Gemara asks whether saying 'Throw' just once is different, and rules that she is not betrothed either way.

kiddushin-12a-14-15.note: A man betrothed a woman with a blue marble stone, and Rav Hisda assessed whether it was worth a peruta, the minimum value needed. It was not, so the betrothal was not valid. The man's mother objected that it had been worth that much on the day of the betrothal, but Rav Hisda replied that she could not make the woman forbidden to other men; if another man betroths her, his betrothal is not cancelled by this earlier one.

terms.meaning: The smallest coin; an item must be worth at least this much to be used for betrothal.

kiddushin-12a-14-15.why: Shmuel has just ruled that an item worth less than a peruta here still makes a doubtful betrothal, since it may be worth more elsewhere. Rav Ḥisda's ruling goes against that, and the Gemara goes on to test it against witnesses in Idit who could say what the stone was worth.

kiddushin-12b-10-10.note: A man betrothed a woman with a mat woven of myrtle branches. People told him it was not worth a peruta, so he said: Let her be betrothed with the four dinars wrapped inside it. She took the mat and said nothing. Rava ruled that silence after the money has already been given means nothing. Scholars in Pum Nahara challenged his proof, Rav Aḥai answered them, and Rav Aḥa bar Rav sent the question to Ravina. Ravina replied: We never heard that objection, but you who heard it should take the possible betrothal seriously.
kiddushin-12b-10-10.why: The Gemara is gathering cases on when a woman's silence counts as agreeing to betrothal; the next case, a woman whose snatched belt is handed back to her, raises the same question.

people.name: Rava
people.about: Rules that silence after the money is given is not consent.

people.name: Rav Huna, son of Rav Yehoshua
people.about: The Sage in whose name the scholars of Pum Nahara challenge Rava.

people.name: Rav Aḥai
people.about: Answers that challenge: not every woman knows the law.

people.name: Rav Aḥa bar Rav
people.about: Sends the question to Ravina.

people.name: Ravina
people.about: Replies that those who heard the objection should be concerned about a betrothal.

terms.meaning: The smallest coin of value; a betrothal gift must be worth at least this much.
A teaching of the early Sages that was left out of the Mishna, the first written collection of Jewish law.

kiddushin-13a-3-3.note: A woman was selling belts and a man snatched one. When she asked for it back, he said he would give it only if she became betrothed to him. She took it and stayed silent. Rav Nahman ruled that she could say she was just taking her own property back, so her silence does not show she agreed to be betrothed.

terms.meaning: Kiddushin, the formal act of engagement, which legally makes a woman a man's wife.

kiddushin-13a-3-3.why: It follows the debate on whether a woman's silence counts as consent. Rava then challenges Rav Naḥman with a teaching that a woman is betrothed with a coin snatched from her, and Rav Naḥman answers that there the couple had already arranged the marriage.

kiddushin-22b-18-18.note: Rabbi Yehuda from India, a convert with no heirs, was dying. Mar Zutra asked the man's slave to carry his shoes to Mar Zutra's house, a way of claiming the slave, since a convert's property without heirs goes to whoever claims it first. One account says the slave was an adult, so Rabbi Yehuda went to death and Mar Zutra gained a slave. Another says the slave was a minor and Mar Zutra was following Abba Shaul, who holds that minor slaves can be claimed by others.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda from India
people.about: a convert who had no heirs

terms.meaning: A teaching from the time of the Mishnah that was not included in it.

kiddushin-22b-18-18.why: The Gemara has just said a master acquires a slave when the slave does labor for him, such as carrying him. Mar Zutra has the slave carry his shoes, an act of service, while the owner is still alive.

kiddushin-25a-1-3.note: The elders of Nezonya stopped coming to Rav Ḥisda's lectures, and he sent Rav Hamnuna to ostracize them. Rav Hamnuna asked them why they stayed away. They said Rav Ḥisda had not answered a question of theirs, so Rav Hamnuna invited them to ask him. They asked: if a master castrates his slave, does the slave go free, as he would for a visible injury? Rav Hamnuna did not know. They mocked his name: not Hamnuna, a hot fish, but Karnuna, a cold one. He went back to Rav Ḥisda, who told him the answer was in a teaching they could have cited, and began to quote it.
kiddushin-25a-1-3.why: The Gemara is listing injuries that free a slave when his master causes them, like an eye or an extra finger. The elders' question adds castration, and the teaching Rav Ḥisda points to lists the body's extremities and, in Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's view, castration as well.

people.name: Rav Ḥisda
people.about: A Sage whose lectures the elders of Nezonya stop attending.

people.name: Rav Hamnuna
people.about: Sent by Rav Ḥisda to ostracize the elders; cannot answer their question.

people.name: the elders of Nezonya
people.about: Local scholars who stay away from Rav Ḥisda's lectures.

terms.meaning: To place someone under a ban that cuts them off from the community until they make amends.
A visible injury to a slave's body; a master who causes one must set the slave free.
A teaching from the Mishna, the first written collection of Jewish law.
In the laws of skin disease, a patch of healthy flesh inside a diseased spot that makes a person ritually impure.

kiddushin-26b-2-2.note: A man from Madon was ill in Jerusalem and wanted to give away a large amount of movable goods as a gift, but had no time for the recipient to take possession by the usual act of pulling. The Sages told him the only way was to transfer them along with land. He acquired a small plot and declared that a part of it, with a hundred sheep and a hundred barrels, was given to the recipient. He died, and the Sages carried out his gift.

terms.meaning: Goods that can be carried, as opposed to land.
A way of taking ownership of movable goods by drawing them toward oneself.

kiddushin-26b-2-2.why: The Gemara is asking whether movable goods must be piled on the land to be acquired along with it. This case is brought as proof that they need not be, since a hundred sheep could not fit on so small a plot. The Gemara rejects the proof by reading 'sela' as rock-hard land, not a tiny one.

kiddushin-26b-4-5.note: Rav Yehuda reported in Rav's name the case of a man in Jerusalem, sick by one account and healthy by another, who owned a great deal of movable property and wanted to give it away. The Sages told him the only way was to transfer it along with land. He bought a small plot near Jerusalem and said: This square handbreadth goes to so-and-so, and with it a hundred sheep and a hundred barrels. Then he died, and the Sages carried out his words.
kiddushin-26b-4-5.why: This is a second attempt to prove that goods need not be piled on the land to pass with it. The Gemara answers that the gift may have been money, which fits on a tiny plot, and then argues over why he could not have used another method.

people.name: Rav Yehuda
people.about: Reports the case in Rav's name.

people.name: Rav
people.about: The Sage whose account Rav Yehuda passes on.

terms.meaning: Goods that can be moved, such as animals and barrels, as opposed to land.
A measure of about the width of a hand, roughly 8 to 10 cm.
Two sides of an argument over how a dying person may give property away; the two accounts of the man's health match their two views.

kiddushin-29b-10-12.note: A teaching says that a father who wants to study Torah takes precedence over his son, unless the son is sharp. Rav Aha bar Ya'akov sent his son to Abaye, found that his studies were not sharp, and decided to go and study himself. Abaye knew that a demon in his study hall harmed visitors. He told the townspeople to give Rav Aha no lodging, hoping that a righteous man might kill it. Rav Aha spent the night there. The demon appeared as a seven-headed serpent, and with each bow of his prayer one head fell off until it died. The next day Rav Aha told the townspeople that without a miracle they would have put him in danger.

people.name: Rav Ya'akov
people.about: his son

terms.meaning: A harmful spirit that the Talmud treats as a real danger.

kiddushin-29b-10-12.why: A teaching of the Sages says that when father and son both want to study, the father comes first, unless the son is quick and sharp. This story is told as an example: the father judges his son not sharp enough and goes to study himself.

kiddushin-29b-15-15.note: Rav Ḥisda kept praising Rav Hamnuna to Rav Huna as a great man. Rav Huna asked that he be sent to him. When Rav Hamnuna arrived, Rav Huna saw that he wore no head cloth, as scholars did, and asked why. Rav Hamnuna said it was because he was not married. Rav Huna turned his face away and said: See that you do not see my face until you marry. Further sayings follow: someone says he would tell the Satan 'an arrow in your eye', and Rava tells Rabbi Natan bar Ami to marry off his son while he still has authority over him, between sixteen and twenty-two or eighteen and twenty-four.
kiddushin-29b-15-15.why: The Gemara has just asked whether a man should study Torah first or marry first, and Shmuel ruled to marry first. Rav Huna's rebuke of the unmarried scholar shows that ruling put into practice.

people.name: Rav Ḥisda
people.about: Praises Rav Hamnuna to Rav Huna.

people.name: Rav Huna
people.about: Rebukes Rav Hamnuna for being unmarried.

people.name: Rav Hamnuna
people.about: A praised scholar who is not yet married.

people.name: Rava
people.about: Advises Rabbi Natan bar Ami to find his son a wife.

people.name: Rabbi Natan bar Ami
people.about: Receives Rava's advice about his son.

terms.meaning: Here, the evil inclination, the urge to sin.

kiddushin-30a-7-7.note: Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba saw Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi hurrying his child to the synagogue to study, with only a cheap cover on his head. Asked why the rush, Rabbi Yehoshua pointed out that the verse about teaching your sons sits right next to the verse about standing at Mount Sinai. After that, Rabbi Hiyya would not eat breakfast until he had studied with his child, and Rabba bar Rav Huna would not eat before bringing his child to the study hall.

terms.meaning: Another name for Mount Sinai, where the Torah was given.

kiddushin-30a-7-7.why: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi has just taught that whoever teaches his grandson Torah is credited as if he received it at Mount Sinai. Here he is seen acting on his own teaching, and it changes the habits of others.

kiddushin-31a-7-9.note: When the Sages asked how far one must go to honor parents, they were told to look at Dama ben Netina, a non-Jew of Ashkelon. He turned down a huge profit from the Sages because the key to the goods lay under his sleeping father's head and he would not wake him. The next year a red heifer, which the Jewish people needed, was born in his herd. He asked only for the money he had lost out of respect for his father.

people.name: Dama ben Netina
people.about: a non-Jew from Ashkelon

terms.meaning: A rare reddish cow whose ashes were used in a purification ritual in the Torah.
A commandment from the Torah.

kiddushin-31a-7-9.why: Just before, Ulla taught that the nations accepted God's words once they heard 'Honor your father and your mother'. The question of how far that duty goes leads to this story, and afterward Rabbi Ḥanina argues that one who is commanded and obeys is greater than a gentile like Dama.

kiddushin-31a-12-12.note: Rav Dimi reported that once Dama ben Netina was wearing a cloak of gold and sitting among the nobles of Rome. His mother came, tore the cloak off him, struck him on the head and spat in his face, and he did not shame her.
kiddushin-31a-12-12.why: The Gemara has been telling of Dama ben Netina as the model of honoring parents. After his honor of his father, this account shows how far he went in honoring his mother.

people.name: Rav Dimi
people.about: Brings this account of Dama ben Netina.

people.name: Dama ben Netina
people.about: A gentile whose patience with his mother is the model of honoring parents.

kiddushin-31b-1-2.note: Rabbi Abbahu said his son Avimi honored his parents perfectly. Though Avimi and five of his sons were ordained to rule on law, he ran to open the door for his father and called out 'Yes, yes' before arriving. Once, when his father fell asleep after asking for water, Avimi stood over him until he woke, and as a reward God helped him interpret Psalm 79.

people.name: Avimi
people.about: Rabbi Abbahu's son

terms.meaning: Formally authorized as a rabbi to give legal rulings.

kiddushin-31b-1-2.why: Avimi has just taught that one son may feed his father pheasant and lose the World to Come while another sets him to grinding and earns it; his father now holds Avimi up as the son who honors properly.

kiddushin-31b-4-4.note: Rabbi Tarfon would bend over so his mother could step onto him to get into and out of her bed. He boasted of this in the study hall, but the Sages told him he had not yet done even half of what honoring her requires. They asked whether she had ever thrown a purse into the sea in front of him without his embarrassing her.

terms.meaning: The place where rabbis gathered to learn and discuss Torah.

kiddushin-31b-4-4.why: The Gemara is collecting examples of how far the duty to honor parents goes, after Avimi stood over his sleeping father; this story shows that even extraordinary service can fall short of the full measure.

kiddushin-31b-6-8.note: Rav Asi's elderly mother kept making demands, asking for jewelry, a husband, and then one as handsome as her son. He realized she was senile and left for the Land of Israel. When he heard she was following him, he asked Rabbi Yohanan if he could leave to greet her. Rabbi Yohanan said only 'May God return you in peace,' which Rabbi Elazar said meant permission. On his way, Rav Asi heard her coffin was arriving and said that had he known, he would not have left.

terms.meaning: The Land of Israel.
Jewish law, or what the law says on a given question.

kiddushin-31b-6-8.why: Rabbi Yohanan has just said it is fortunate never to have seen one's parents, so hard is it to honor them properly; Rav Asi's story shows that strain, and the Gemara then turns to how one honors a parent in life and in death.

kiddushin-32b-1-1.note: At his son's wedding celebration, Rava himself served drinks to the guests. When he poured a cup for Rav Pappa and Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua, they stood up before him. When he poured for Rav Mari and Rav Pinehas son of Rav Hisda, they did not stand. Rava became angry and said: Are these rabbis real Sages, and those not Sages?
kiddushin-32b-1-1.why: Rav Yosef and Rava have said that a teacher who waives the honor due to him has it waived. The Gemara raises this story as a challenge: Rava served his guests, yet was angry when Sages did not stand for him.

people.name: Rava
people.about: A Sage who served drinks at his son's wedding and was angered when two guests did not stand for him.

people.name: Rav Pappa
people.about: A guest at the wedding who stood when Rava poured for him.

people.name: Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua
people.about: A guest who stood when Rava poured for him.

people.name: Rav Mari
people.about: A guest who did not stand for Rava.

people.name: Rav Pinehas son of Rav Hisda
people.about: A guest who did not stand for Rava.

kiddushin-32b-2-2.note: At the wedding of his son Abba Mar, Rav Pappa served drinks to the guests. He poured a cup for Rav Yitzhak, son of Rav Yehuda, who did not stand up for him, and Rav Pappa became angry. The passage concludes that a rabbi may give up the honor due him, but others should still show some sign of respect, such as getting ready to stand.

people.name: Abba Mar
people.about: Rav Pappa's son

people.name: Rav Yitzhak, son of Rav Yehuda

kiddushin-32b-2-2.why: This is a second challenge, after Rava's wedding, to the view that a teacher can waive his honor. The Gemara answers that even when he waives it, others must still show him some act of reverence.

kiddushin-32b-3-5.note: Rav Ashi held that a Nasi, unlike a rabbi, cannot give up the honor due him. The Gemara challenges this with a story. At the wedding of Rabban Gamliel's son, Rabban Gamliel, then Nasi of the Sanhedrin, stood and served drinks to Rabbi Eliezer, Rabbi Yehoshua and Rabbi Tzadok. Rabbi Eliezer refused the cup, Rabbi Yehoshua accepted it, and Eliezer objected. Rabbi Yehoshua answered that Abraham, a greater man, served his guests, and Rabbi Tzadok added that God Himself provides for every creature. The story, raised as an objection to Rav Ashi, suggests that even a Nasi may give up the honor due him.

people.name: Rabban Gamliel
people.about: Nasi of the Sanhedrin at the time

terms.meaning: The president or leader of the Sanhedrin, the highest Jewish court.

kiddushin-32b-3-5.why: Rav Ashi has said that even if a rabbi may waive his honor, a Nasi may not. The Gemara cites this incident against him, since the Nasi served and the Sages accepted; afterward Rav Ashi's rule is restated as applying to a king.

kiddushin-33a-6-6.note: Bar Kappara (or, some say, Rabbi Shmuel bar Rabbi Yosei) was sitting in a bathhouse and did not stand when Rabbi Shimon, the son of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, passed by. Rabbi Shimon told his father he had taught the man part of Torat Kohanim and was still not honored. His father suggested that the man might have been thinking over what he had learned and did not see him come in.

people.name: Rabbi Shimon bar Rabbi
people.about: son of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi

terms.meaning: An ancient teaching-commentary on the Book of Leviticus.

kiddushin-33a-6-6.why: A teaching said one need not stand for an elder in a bathhouse. The Gemara cites this story as a challenge: the father excused the student only because he was lost in thought, implying one must stand even there.

kiddushin-33a-13-13.note: Abaye was riding a donkey along the bank of the Sagya River. Rav Mesharshiyya and other rabbis on the other bank did not stand for him. Abaye asked whether he was not their main teacher and so deserved to be honored even from afar. They replied that it had not occurred to them, because they had not seen him.
kiddushin-33a-13-13.why: Abaye has just ruled that one stands for an ordinary elder only within four cubits, but for one's primary teacher as soon as he comes into view; both incidents show that rule in practice.

kiddushin-33a-15-15.note: Ravina was sitting with Rabbi Yirmeya of Difti when a man passed by without covering his head, and Ravina called him rude for not honoring a rabbi. Rabbi Yirmeya suggested the man might be from Mata Mehasya, a city with so many rabbis that people there are less careful about showing such respect.
kiddushin-33a-15-15.why: The discussion is about the respect owed to Sages and teachers; Rabbi Yirmeya suggests that someone used to seeing rabbis every day may not show it, so the lapse need not be rudeness.

kiddushin-39a-10-11.note: Rav Hanan and Rav Anan were traveling outside the Land of Israel and saw a man planting different kinds of seeds together. One suggested ostracizing him for a forbidden act, but the other said these laws were not clear to him. They then saw a man planting wheat and barley among grapevines. The same objection was raised, and the answer was that by Rabbi Yoshiya's view, one is liable by Torah law only if he sows wheat, barley and a grape seed in a single hand motion, so this man should not be ostracized.

terms.meaning: Kilayim, the Torah's ban on mixing certain kinds of seeds when planting.
To formally shut someone out of the community as a punishment.

kiddushin-39a-10-11.why: The Gemara has just said that the ban on sowing mixed seeds applies only in the Land of Israel, while grafting different trees is banned everywhere; this story shows Sages declining to punish a man for mixed sowing.

kiddushin-39b-13-13.note: One account of how Aher went astray: he saw the tongue of Hutzpit the disseminator, who, as the translation explains, had been executed by the government, being dragged along by 'something else', a euphemism for a pig. Aher said: Shall a mouth that produced pearls lick the dust? And he went out and sinned.
kiddushin-39b-13-13.why: Rav Yosef said Aher would not have sinned had he read the Torah's promise of reward as referring to the World-to-Come. The Gemara asks what made him sin and gives this as a second answer, after the boy who died doing a mitzva.

people.name: Aher
people.about: Literally 'Other', the name given to the Sage Elisha ben Avuya after he abandoned the Torah.

people.name: Hutzpit the disseminator
people.about: A Sage whose tongue Aher saw dragged in the dirt after his death.

terms.meaning: The speaker who repeated and explained a Sage's lecture aloud to the audience.

kiddushin-39b-15-15.note: A noblewoman tried to seduce Rabbi Hanina bar Pappi. He used a spoken formula to cover himself in boils so she would be repelled, but she used magic to heal him. He fled and hid overnight in a bathhouse so dangerous that two people entering together were harmed even by day. The next day the Sages asked who had protected him, and he said angels in the form of two soldiers had guarded him all night. The Sages suggested that perhaps he had been tempted toward forbidden intercourse and resisted, since a miracle is done for anyone who resists such temptation. They cited a verse they read as referring to people like Rabbi Tzadok and his colleagues.

people.name: Rabbi Tzadok
people.about: given as an example of the kind of person the closing verse refers to, someone saved from such temptation

terms.meaning: a noblewoman, a woman of high social standing.
a soldier of the emperor, an imperial guard.

kiddushin-39b-15-15.why: Rava has just explained that one who 'sits and does not sin' is rewarded when a chance to sin comes to him and he resists it; this story illustrates such a person.

kiddushin-40a-1-1.note: A noblewoman tried to seduce Rabbi Tzadok. He said he was too weak and needed food, and she offered non-kosher food. He said the one who commits this act would eat such food too, and when she lit the oven to roast it, he climbed into the oven. He explained that the one who does this act falls into the fires of Gehenna (hell). She replied that had she known how serious it was to him, she would not have caused him such distress.

terms.meaning: the place of fiery punishment after death, roughly like hell.

kiddushin-40a-1-1.why: The Sages have just taught that a miracle is done for whoever escapes a forbidden sexual temptation, and cited a verse about 'mighty' people such as Rabbi Tzadok and his colleagues; this is the story that phrase refers to.

kiddushin-40a-2-2.note: Rav Kahana sold palm-leaf baskets to women, and a noblewoman tried to seduce him. He said he would first go adorn himself, climbed to the roof, and fell off. Elijah the prophet caught him and complained that saving him meant traveling four hundred parasangs. Rav Kahana answered that poverty, which forced him into a trade that brought him near women, was the cause, and Elijah gave him a basket full of dinars so he would not have to keep selling.

people.name: Elijah the prophet
people.about: the biblical prophet, who in Jewish tradition appears to rescue people

terms.meaning: an ancient Persian unit of distance, a few miles.
a coin of the period.

kiddushin-40a-2-2.why: It is the last in a series of stories about Sages who resisted seduction and were saved by a miracle, illustrating the teaching that whoever escapes a forbidden sexual temptation has a miracle done for him.

kiddushin-45b-3-3.note: A husband and wife disagreed over whom to marry their young daughter to: he wanted his relative, she wanted hers. She pressed him until he said: Let her be for your relative. But while they were eating and drinking at the meal, his relative came onto the roof and betrothed the girl to himself.
kiddushin-45b-3-3.why: The Gemara is asking when a minor betrothed without her father's consent is still betrothed because he secretly wanted it. Abaye says this father kept his word to his wife; Rava says no one prepares a feast and then lets it go to waste.

terms.meaning: The first stage of Jewish marriage, done by giving the woman (or a minor girl's father) money or an object of value; for a minor, it depends on her father's wish.

kiddushin-50a-9-9.note: A man sold his property after telling the buyer he planned to move to the Land of Israel. He went but could not settle there, came back to Babylonia, and tried to cancel the sale. Rava ruled that people go to Israel intending to settle, so since he could not, he can cancel the sale. A second version of the tradition says Rava ruled the opposite: he intended to go and did go, so the sale stands.

people.name: Rava
people.about: a Babylonian sage

terms.meaning: the Land of Israel.

kiddushin-50a-9-9.why: The Gemara has just argued that unspoken intentions do not count in a transaction. Here the seller stated his reason aloud, and the question becomes how far that stated purpose reaches.

kiddushin-50a-10-10.note: A similar case: a man sold his property intending to move to the Land of Israel but never went. Rav Ashi ruled the sale stands, since he could have gone had he wanted and the matter was up to him. A second version words this as a question. The Gemara says the two versions differ only if something outside his control stopped him: the first version still upholds the sale, the second implies it would be cancelled.

terms.meaning: the Talmud's discussion and analysis that builds on the Mishnah.

kiddushin-50a-10-10.why: It follows the case of a seller who went but could not settle. The Gemara explains that the two versions of Rav Ashi's words differ over a man stopped on the way by circumstances beyond his control.

kiddushin-52b-12-14.note: After Rabbi Meir died, Rabbi Yehuda told his students not to let Rabbi Meir's students in, calling them quarrelsome men who came not to learn but to overwhelm him with laws. Sumakhos, a student of Rabbi Meir, pushed his way in and reported Rabbi Meir's teaching that a priest who betroths a woman with his share of the offerings has not betrothed her. Rabbi Yehuda grew angry, repeated his warning, and objected that a woman is never in the Temple courtyard. Rabbi Yosei said: People will say Meir died, Yehuda grew angry and Yosei was silent; what will become of the Torah? He answered that a father can accept betrothal for his daughter there, a woman can send an agent, and she might push in.
kiddushin-52b-12-14.why: The mishna rules that a priest cannot betroth a woman with his portion of the offerings; this teaching gives that ruling as Rabbi Meir taught it, and the Gemara goes on to the dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Yosei.

people.name: Rabbi Meir
people.about: A Sage who had died; his teaching is reported by his student.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda
people.about: A Sage who barred Rabbi Meir's students from his study hall.

people.name: Sumakhos
people.about: A student of Rabbi Meir who pushed his way in.

people.name: Rabbi Yosei
people.about: A Sage present who answered Rabbi Yehuda's objection.

terms.meaning: The parts of sacrificed animals given to priests to eat. Some, of the most sacred order, could be eaten only inside the Temple courtyard.
To perform the first stage of marriage, usually by giving the woman money or an object of value.
The inner area of the Temple in Jerusalem where sacrifices were offered and the holiest portions eaten.

kiddushin-57a-0-1.note: Shimon HaAmasoni (some say Nehemya HaAmasoni) used to draw a teaching from every 'et' in the Torah. When he reached the verse 'You shall fear et the Lord your God', he stopped, since, as the translation explains, nothing can be feared alongside God. His students asked: What will become of all the 'et's you have interpreted? He said: Just as I was rewarded for interpreting, I am rewarded for withdrawing. This stood until Rabbi Akiva came and taught that the 'et' in that verse includes Torah scholars.
kiddushin-57a-0-1.why: The Gemara has just said that one Sage does not draw laws from the word 'et', and cites this teaching to show that this was a real method of reading that a Sage could give up.

people.name: Shimon HaAmasoni
people.about: A Sage who drew teachings from every 'et' in the Torah, then withdrew; some name him Nehemya HaAmasoni.

people.name: Rabbi Akiva
people.about: A Sage who later read the 'et' in 'You shall fear the Lord your God' as including Torah scholars.

terms.meaning: A small Hebrew word that marks the object of a verb and has no meaning of its own; some Sages read it as adding something extra to a verse.

kiddushin-59a-5-7.note: Rav Giddel was in the middle of buying a plot of land when Rabbi Abba bought it. Rav Giddel's complaint passed through Rabbi Zeira to Rav Yitzhak Nappaha, who asked Rabbi Abba whether it is wrong to snatch a poor man's found loaf; Abba said the taker is wicked. Abba said he had not known of Giddel's attempt but would not sell the land, his first purchase, though he would give it as a gift. Giddel would not take a gift, and Abba then would not take the land either, so it was called the land of the Sages.

terms.meaning: one of the three holidays when Jews traditionally traveled to the Temple, here a time when scholars gathered.

kiddushin-59a-5-7.why: The Gemara has been telling of agents who bought for themselves what they were sent to get for another; this story extends the theme to someone who takes a deal another person is already pursuing.

kiddushin-66a-5-5.note: The Sages ask what happens if one witness tells a husband his wife was unfaithful and he stays silent. Abaye says the witness is believed; Rava says not, since such matters need two witnesses. Abaye points to a case: a blind man's messenger reported seeing the blind man's wife commit adultery, and Mar Shmuel told him to divorce her if he trusted the messenger, otherwise not.

terms.meaning: Jewish law; the accepted ruling.

kiddushin-66a-5-5.why: The Sages asked whether one witness is believed when he tells a husband his wife committed adultery and the husband is silent. Abaye says yes and cites this case; Rava reads Mar Shmuel as meaning trusted like two witnesses.

kiddushin-66a-7-11.note: King Yannai conquered sixty cities and held a feast for the Sages. A scoffer, Elazar ben Po'ira, told him that the Sages secretly resented him and suggested making them stand before the High Priest's frontplate the king wore. The elder Yehuda ben Gedidya told Yannai to be content with the crown of kingship and leave the priesthood to Aaron's descendants. His words rested on a rumor that Yannai's mother had been taken captive, which would disqualify him. The rumor was investigated and not confirmed, and in his rage the king expelled the Sages. Elazar urged him to destroy them. Yannai asked what would become of the Torah, and Elazar said it lay wrapped in the corner for anyone to study. The Sages were killed, and the world was empty of Torah until Shimon ben Shatah restored it.

people.name: King Yannai
people.about: a king who was also High Priest, of the priestly Hasmonean family

people.name: Elazar ben Po'ira
people.about: a scoffer present at the feast

people.name: Yehuda ben Gedidya
people.about: an elder present

people.name: Shimon ben Shatah
people.about: restored the Torah afterward

terms.meaning: a priest's child disqualified from the priesthood because of a forbidden marriage in the family line.
the traditional teachings passed down by the Sages alongside the written text.

kiddushin-66a-7-11.why: Abaye holds that a single witness is believed about a wife's adultery and Rava disagrees. Abaye cites this account because the rumor about Yannai's mother was 'investigated and not found', which he reads as one witness believed unless two contradict him.

kiddushin-70a-11-16.note: A man from Neharde'a, told at a butcher shop in Pumbedita to wait until Rav Yehuda's servant had been served, mocked Rav Yehuda with an insulting nickname. Rav Yehuda excommunicated him and, told that the man habitually called people slaves, proclaimed that he himself was a slave. The man summoned Rav Yehuda to Rav Nahman's court, and Rav Huna advised him to go out of respect for the Exilarch's house. At Rav Nahman's home Rav Yehuda corrected nearly everything his host said: his words for a fence, a bench, a citron and a cup, his offer to have his daughter Donag pour drinks, and his offer to send greetings to his wife Yalta. Yalta sent word to Rav Nahman to finish with him. How the case itself ended is not told here.
kiddushin-70a-11-16.why: The Gemara has just quoted the teaching that whoever calls others flawed in lineage is himself flawed, with Shmuel's comment; this man, who called people slaves, is the case where Rav Yehuda acted on it.

people.name: Rav Yehuda bar Yehezkel
people.about: A Sage in Pumbedita whose servant is served first; he excommunicates the man and declares him a slave.

people.name: Rav Nahman
people.about: A judge in Neharde'a before whom the man summons Rav Yehuda.

people.name: Rav Huna
people.about: Advises Rav Yehuda to answer the summons.

people.name: Donag
people.about: Rav Nahman's daughter, a minor.

people.name: Yalta
people.about: Rav Nahman's wife, who tells him to end the exchange.

terms.meaning: To put a person under a formal ban that cuts him off from the community.
The head of the Jewish community in Babylonia. Rav Nahman was linked to his household, so ignoring Rav Nahman's summons would slight it.
Saying a man descends from non-Jewish slaves, which meant he could not marry a Jew of unflawed lineage.

kiddushin-70b-1-8.note: Rav Yehuda has come to Rav Nahman's court in Neharde'a, summoned by a man he excommunicated and declared a slave. He explained that the man had insulted a Sage's agent and habitually called people slaves. The man arrived, protesting that he came from the Hasmonean kings; Rav Yehuda quoted Shmuel that anyone who says so is a slave. When Rav Nahman objected to a ruling quoted after the fact, Rav Mattana, arriving that day after thirteen years away, confirmed it: the last Hasmonean girl had cried this from a roof, then fell and died. The man was proclaimed a slave and several marriage contracts were torn up. Townspeople chased Rav Yehuda to stone him; he threatened to reveal Shmuel's list of flawed families, and they threw down the stones, which dammed the Malka River.
kiddushin-70b-1-8.why: The Gemara is listing families of flawed lineage; in this hearing Rav Nahman presses whether Shmuel's teaching lets one only suspect a man who calls others slaves, or also proclaim him one.

people.name: Rav Yehuda
people.about: A Sage from Pumbedita, summoned to court for declaring a man a slave.

people.name: Rav Nahman
people.about: The judge in Neharde'a who hears the case.

people.name: Rav Mattana
people.about: A Sage, back in Neharde'a after thirteen years, who confirms what Shmuel said.

terms.meaning: A royal family of priests. In Shmuel's teaching, none of them survived except slaves and one girl, so a claim to descend from them marks a man as a slave.
The document a husband gives his wife at marriage (ketubah). Tearing them up meant those marriages were treated as invalid.
To put a person under a formal ban that cuts him off from the community.

kiddushin-71a-4-5.note: In Rabbi Pinehas's day, people wanted to declare the lineage of Babylonian families doubtful compared to the Land of Israel's. Rabbi Pinehas told his servants that once he had made two statements in the house of study, they should pick him up on a stretcher and run. He first announced that slaughtering a bird is not required by Torah law, and while the scholars were absorbed in that, he declared that the Land of Israel's lineage is muddled compared to Babylonia's. His servants carried him off, and his pursuers could not catch him. The scholars then examined families' lineage until they reached ones too dangerous to accuse, and stopped.
kiddushin-71a-4-5.why: The Gemara has just quoted the teaching that Babylonian lineage is purer than the Land of Israel's, and told how Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi resisted the opposite claim; this is a second attempt at that claim, met the same way.

people.name: Rabbi Pinehas
people.about: A Sage who declares the Land of Israel's lineage muddled compared to Babylonia's, then has himself carried away.

terms.meaning: Family descent. A flaw in it, such as descent from a forbidden union, could bar a person from marrying into other families.
Mixed with families of doubtful descent, so that marrying into them would require checking first.
The hall where the Sages and their students met to learn and debate.

kiddushin-71b-2-2.note: Ze'eiri, a Babylonian, was avoiding Rabbi Yohanan, who kept urging him to marry his daughter. When Ze'eiri carried Rabbi Yohanan over a puddle, Rabbi Yohanan asked why he honored their Torah but not their daughters. Rabbi Yohanan argued that worry about flawed Jewish ancestry in Eretz Yisrael is no reason, since people of flawed lineage also stayed in Babylonia. The Gemara then notes he forgot a teaching of Rabbi Elazar that those who stayed in Babylonia were all of sound lineage.

people.name: Ze'eiri
people.about: a Babylonian Sage

people.name: Rabbi Yohanan
people.about: a Sage from Eretz Yisrael

terms.meaning: A person of flawed lineage under Jewish law, born from certain forbidden unions.
The Land of Israel.

kiddushin-71b-2-2.why: The Gemara has just said that anyone who speaks like a Babylonian may marry without having his lineage checked, since Babylonian families are presumed unflawed; here a Babylonian Sage holds back from marrying into a family of the Land of Israel.

kiddushin-71b-4-8.note: Ulla visited Pumbedita and saw that Rav Yehuda's grown son Rav Yitzhak was unmarried. Rav Yehuda said he worried about finding a woman of sound lineage. Ulla replied that none of us can be sure of our own ancestry, since we may descend from women assaulted during wars or from people the prophet Amos condemned, and Rabbi Abbahu says some descend from wife-swapping groups, which produces mamzerim. When Rav Yehuda asked how to tell, Ulla said to follow the silence. In the Land of Israel, when two people quarrel, the one who goes silent first is considered to be of finer lineage.

people.name: Rav Yitzhak
people.about: Rav Yehuda's son

terms.meaning: a person born from certain forbidden unions, who is restricted in whom they may marry.

kiddushin-71b-4-8.why: The Gemara is discussing how to know which families have unflawed lineage; Ulla's advice gives a practical test, which Rav then applies to Babylonia in the lines that follow.

kiddushin-73a-5-5.note: Rabbi Zeira taught in Mehoza that a convert may marry a mamzeret, and everyone pelted him with their etrogim because the many converts felt insulted. Rava said he should have been more careful in a place with many converts. Rava first taught there that a convert may marry a priest's daughter, and they carried him on silk. He then taught the mamzeret ruling, and they said he had lost the honor of his first sermon. Rava answered that he had done what was good for them: a convert may marry from pure lineage or from a mamzeret, as he wishes.

terms.meaning: a woman born from certain forbidden unions, who is restricted in whom she may marry.
a citron, the fruit used on the holiday of Sukkot.

kiddushin-73a-5-5.why: The Gemara has just cited support for Rav's view that priests' daughters may marry men barred from the priesthood, after debating whether converts may marry a mamzeret; Rava's two teachings state both rulings, which the Gemara then adopts as law.

kiddushin-76b-9-10.note: Rav Adda bar Ahava's host, a convert's son, and Rav Beivai both wanted the city's official position, so they went to Rav Yosef. Rav Yosef cited a verse about appointing a king 'from among your brothers' to show that a convert cannot hold official positions. Rav Adda asked about someone whose mother is born Jewish, and Rav Yosef said the verse allows it. He ruled that Rav Beivai, a great Torah scholar, oversee religious matters and the host oversee the city's other matters. Abaye's moral was to host someone like Rav Adda bar Ahava, whose pleading won his host his post.

people.name: Rav Adda bar Ahava
people.about: his host's advocate in this story

people.name: Rav Beivai
people.about: described as a great man in Torah learning

people.name: Rav Yosef
people.about: the sage who decided the dispute

people.name: Abaye
people.about: gave the moral of the story

terms.meaning: someone not born Jewish who joined the Jewish people.

kiddushin-76b-9-10.why: The mishna says anyone whose ancestors held public posts may marry into the priesthood without checking, and the Gemara asks whether people of flawed lineage are ever appointed; this case shows who may hold a post.

kiddushin-80a-4-4.note: A woman came to Jerusalem with a child riding on her shoulders, as a mother would, and raised him. He later had intercourse with her, and the court stoned them for the prohibition on a mother and son. The text says this was not because he was definitely her son, since there was no testimony of that, but because he clung to her and so had the presumed status of her son.

people.name: Rabbi Shimon ben Pazi
people.about: passed the story down

people.name: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi
people.about: passed the story down

people.name: Bar Kappara
people.about: the source of the account

terms.meaning: treating a person as having a certain status because of how things appear, even without proof.

kiddushin-80a-4-4.why: Rabbi Yohanan holds that a court may flog, stone or burn on the basis of presumed status alone, without witnesses to the family tie; this incident is cited as a death sentence resting on such a presumption.

kiddushin-81a-10-11.note: Captive women who had been redeemed were lodged in the upper room of Rav Amram the Pious's house, and the ladder was removed to keep men from them. One woman was so beautiful that it seemed a light shone from the doorway, and Rav Amram lifted a ladder that ten men could not lift and began to climb. Halfway up, he braced himself and shouted that his house was on fire. The Sages came and said he had embarrassed them. He replied that it was better for them to be shamed in his house in this world than to be ashamed of him in the World-to-Come. He then swore that his evil inclination should leave him, and it came out of him like a pillar of fire. He told it that although it was fire and he was only flesh, he had beaten it.

terms.meaning: the inner urge toward sin that Jewish tradition says every person struggles with.
the afterlife, where a person's deeds are judged.

kiddushin-81a-10-11.why: The Gemara has been discussing how to keep men and women from being alone together, with Abaye and Rava setting up barriers and Avin warning that festivals are the dangerous time; this story shows even a pious Sage nearly overcome.

kiddushin-81a-12-12.note: Rabbi Meir used to mock sinners by saying it is easy to resist temptation. One day Satan appeared to him as a woman across a river, and Meir crossed a rope bridge toward her. Halfway across, the evil inclination left him and said that if heaven did not proclaim "be careful with Rabbi Meir and his Torah," it would have made his blood worth two small coins. The passage ends there.

terms.meaning: in rabbinic tradition, the force that tempts people to sin.
a very small coin.

kiddushin-81a-12-12.why: The Gemara is discussing the pull of temptation between men and women; after Rav Amram's struggle it tells of Sages who scoffed at sinners and were shown how close they came to falling.

kiddushin-81a-13-13.note: Rabbi Akiva, too, used to ridicule people who sinned. One day Satan appeared to him as a woman at the top of a palm tree, and Akiva grabbed the tree and began to climb. Halfway up, the evil inclination left him and said that if it were not proclaimed in heaven to take care of Rabbi Akiva and his Torah, it would have made his blood worth no more than two small coins.

terms.meaning: the inner urge toward sin that Jewish tradition says every person struggles with.
a very small coin.

kiddushin-81a-13-13.why: This is the second of a run of stories, after Rabbi Meir's, about Sages who scoffed at sinners and were shown how close they came to falling, in a discussion of the pull of temptation between men and women.

kiddushin-81a-14-14.note: Peleimu used to say every day, 'An arrow in the eye of Satan.' On the eve of Yom Kippur, Satan came to his door as a poor man asking for food and kept asking to be let in until he sat at Peleimu's table, where he behaved disgustingly and spat into a cup. When people scolded him, he pretended to die, and people cried that Peleimu had killed a man, so Peleimu fled and hid in the bathroom. Satan followed him, revealed himself, and asked why Peleimu kept provoking him. He told Peleimu to say instead, 'Let the Merciful One rebuke the Satan.'

people.name: Peleimu
people.about: a sage

terms.meaning: in rabbinic tradition, the force that tempts people to sin.
the Day of Atonement, the holiest day of the Jewish year.
a common Aramaic way of referring to God.

kiddushin-81a-14-14.why: This follows the accounts of Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Akiva, who mocked sinners and were tested; here a Sage who taunts Satan daily is taught to ask God to rebuke him instead.

kiddushin-81b-1-3.note: Rabbi Hiyya bar Ashi would pray each day to be saved from the evil inclination. His wife, who knew he had stayed away from her for years, wondered why he needed to pray that. One day she dressed up, walked past him in the garden, and said she was Haruta, a well-known prostitute. He propositioned her, climbed a tree for a pomegranate as her price, and they had intercourse. At home he sat in the burning oven in guilt, and when she told him it was her, he did not believe her until she gave him proofs. He said he had still intended to sin, fasted for the rest of his life over it, and died in his misery.

people.name: Haruta
people.about: the name his wife gave when posing as a prostitute

terms.meaning: the inner urge toward sin that Jewish tradition says every person struggles with.

kiddushin-81b-1-3.why: Right after this, the Gemara shows from verses that one who meant to sin needs atonement even if no sin took place; Rabbi Hiyya bar Ashi's lifelong fasting puts that idea into a life.

kiddushin-81b-14-14.note: Rav Aha bar Abba visited his son-in-law Rav Hisda and put his granddaughter on his lap. Rav Hisda asked whether she might already be betrothed. Rav Aha replied that if so Rav Hisda had broken Rav's ruling against betrothing a minor daughter. Rav Hisda answered that Rav Aha had broken Shmuel's rule against making use of a woman. Rav Aha answered with another statement of Shmuel that such actions are permitted for the sake of Heaven, meaning out of family affection without any improper element.

people.name: Rav Hisda
people.about: Rav Aha's son-in-law

people.name: Shmuel
people.about: quoted by both sides

terms.meaning: to begin a marriage legally; a girl who has been betrothed is treated as another man's wife.
done with a pure, proper motive.

kiddushin-81b-14-14.why: The Gemara is discussing how close a man may be to young relatives, and Rav Hisda has just ruled that a father may not sleep near a daughter once she is ashamed before him; this story shows where affection toward a granddaughter stands.

kiddushin-80b-11-11.note: The Rabbis are described as concerned about sin even in times of deep grief. As an example, a woman visiting her husband's grave had intercourse with a man guarding the body of someone executed by the king. Meanwhile that body was taken, and she suggested digging up her husband so the guard could claim he had done his job. The point is that even in mourning a person can give in to temptation.

terms.meaning: to dig up a buried body.
